title: Family of mentally ill man who hanged himself in Ottawa jail demands change
article: An inmate who hanged himself in his cell at the Ottawa jail was suffering from schizophrenia and had been off his medication for four months or more before his suicide, according to his grieving sister.

Sigrid Geddes said she believes her younger brother Cleve Geddes - who was known to family and friends by the nickname "Cas" - didn't belong in the Ottawa-Carleton Detention Centre. He belonged in a hospital after struggling with his mental illness for the past decade, she said.

"Why is he locked in there? Obviously he is not right. How can the system disregard lives like this?" asked Geddes Wednesday, a week after her brother hanged himself in his protective custody cell after reportedly being taken off a suicide watch. He died in hospital two days later.
It is the third suicide in the detention centre in the past 10 months.
"Somebody who is on a suicide watch has mental health problems. What do you think it feels like to be locked in a cell?," asked Geddes. "You can't expect anyone to do anything different. It's sick."

Geddes said her brother's tragic death came after she tried to warn his lawyer that he shouldn't be sent to the detention centre following his arrest on Jan. 30 for uttering death threats, resisting arrest and assaulting a police officer.

"He has schizophrenia and everybody knows that. The police station in Killaloe know, the court in Pembroke, I don't understand how they wouldn't know that," said Geddes. "It's all over every record that there is."
Geddes said she was told by a duty counsel lawyer her brother had spent the night in jail in Pembroke.

"I asked why is he at the Pembroke jail, he should be in the hospital. He's sick and they said he may be going to jail. And I'm like 'no, that is not the right place for him. He's mentally ill,'" she said.
Geddes said her brother first showed signs of mental illness about 10 years ago. The family became concerned when he started acting "strange."
Geddes said her brother would speak in riddles, go off on rants and became withdrawn. Geddes said her brother had taken his medication off and on after his diagnosis.

"He hated taking the medication because of the side effects. I don't know if you've every hung out with anybody who is on some heavy duty anti-psychotics, but they kind of turn you into a zombie. That was the issue there," she said.
Geddes had been in trouble before he became sick, his sister said. He spent time in jail in Toronto where he was held in segregation for two weeks.
"That would be a very scary place for someone who is mentally ill to be there for so long," added sister Bronwyn Geddes.

A couple of years ago he was relatively stable, said Sigrid Geddes. He was living in Pembroke, going to college and had a paper route that he walked for five hours a day, but then he started misbehaving and got kicked out of his house.
Geddes said Cas was a different person before the illness.

"He was really amazing when he was younger, just the shining star, just brilliant and athletic and the most funny and just the most amazing brother that anyone could ever wish for. And then he started to get sick," she said.

"I think mostly Cas was very, very upset that he was sick and he was just super, super frustrated," she said. "He was a really bright guy underneath his illness. He was still a human being and he was still Cas."

Geddes said she last saw her brother about two weeks ago, when he came to her place in Wilno to help pile wood. Geddes said they had lunch together, she took him to Barry's Bay to buy him a hockey stick and he hitch hiked back to Killaloe. That was two days before his arrest.
She tried to call him since he ended up in the jail, but he couldn't call her back because she only had a cell phone. Inmates can only collect to a landline.
Geddes said her mother had spoken to him the day before the suicide attempt. "He said he just wanted to get out," said Geddes.
Geddes said the family has been given few details about what happened to her brother.
"They told us that he hung himself and that they found him without a heartbeat. That's the only thing that we know," she said. "We haven't been ready to start asking any questions."

Geddes said the family only learned about the suicide attempt through a Facebook friend. The jail apparently didn't have any emergency contacts for him, so a social worker from the jail looked on Facebook and found one of his friends. That person had her daughter call the family, Geddes said.
At first, Geddes thought her brother had been transferred to the hospital because of his mental illness. When she called, the social worker told her her brother was non-verbal.
"I thought he was just playing head games," she said.

It wasn't until a doctor called that she learned he was on life support in the intensive care unit. When she got to the hospital, she arrived to find two correctional officers guarding her brain-damaged and unconscious brother.
"They were there until he was dead," she said.
The ministry has declined to comment on specifics surrounding her brother's case, citing inmate privacy.

Geddes said she is comforted to know there will be a coroner's inquest into her brother's death, as is required in all cases of inmate suicide, where a jury can make recommendations to prevent similar suicides.
"That jail system is not working very well," she said. "I'd like to see some change. Things need to change."
